How to complete this lesson
Roots undo repeated multiplication

Squaring multiplies a number by itself. Cubing multiplies three copies. A square root or cube root reverses that relationship.

Build the result	Undo it	Geometric meaning
122 = 144	√144 = 12	A square of area 144 has side length 12.
53 = 125	∛125 = 5	A cube of volume 125 has edge length 5.

A perfect square is a whole number that is the square of a whole number. A perfect cube is a whole number that is the cube of a whole number. Learning common examples helps, but prime factorization explains why a number belongs in either group.

WORKED EXAMPLE

Pair the prime factors for a square root

Determine √900 without first reaching for a calculator.

Factor the number.
900 = 22 · 32 · 52

The prime factors can all be grouped into pairs.

Take one from each identical pair.
30 · 30 = (2 · 3 · 5)(2 · 3 · 5)

Each side of the multiplication gets one 2, one 3 and one 5.

State the principal square root.
302 = 900

Therefore √900 = 30. The radical symbol asks for the nonnegative square root, not ±30.

Pairs for squares. Triples for cubes.

In a perfect square’s prime factorization, each exponent is even. In a perfect cube’s prime factorization, each exponent is a multiple of three. This is why checking only the last digit is not a reliable general method.

Number	Prime factorization	What the groups tell us
144	24 · 32	All factors pair: it is a perfect square.
216	23 · 33	All factors form triples: it is a perfect cube.
64	26	Six copies can form pairs or triples: both.
72	23 · 32	A factor is left over in pairs and in triples: neither.

If you are asked which real numbers square to 900, both 30 and −30 work. But √900 by itself means 30. Keep the question and the notation together.

WORKED EXAMPLE

Use a root to find a dimension

A cube-shaped container has volume 1,728 cm³. Find its edge length.

Match volume to the correct operation.
V = s3

A cube has three equal dimensions. A square root would answer an area question, not this volume question.

Group the prime factors in threes.
1728 = 26 · 33

Two groups of three 2s give 2 × 2. One group of three 3s gives 3.

Find and check the edge.
s = 2 · 2 · 3 = 12

Check: 12 × 12 × 12 = 1,728. The edge is 12 cm; a length is not measured in cm³.

When the number is not a perfect power

You can still locate a root between two whole numbers. Since 7² = 49 and 8² = 64, √58 lies between 7 and 8. Since 4³ = 64 and 5³ = 125, ∛100 lies between 4 and 5. An estimate should be consistent with these bounds.

Do not write √58 = 7 just because 7 is the lower whole number. Use “between 7 and 8,” or the approximation symbol when reporting a decimal estimate.

How to complete this lesson
Use both conditions—not just one

For a trinomial whose leading coefficient is 1, expansion gives a useful pattern.

(x + p)(x + q) = x2 + (p + q)x + pq

To factor x² + bx + c, look for integers p and q that multiply to c and add to b. “Monic” means the leading coefficient is 1. This sum/product rule depends on that leading 1; a different leading coefficient needs the method in 3.6.

Write the pair you are trying, then check both conditions. You are not guessing a full answer blindly—you are narrowing a small list of factor pairs.

WORKED EXAMPLE

Build a positive factor pair

Factor x² + 11x + 24.

List factor pairs for the constant.
1 · 24; 2 · 12; 3 · 8; 4 · 6

The signed product must be 24. Since the middle term is positive, start with positive pairs.

Choose the pair with sum 11.
3 + 8 = 11

The other sums are 25, 14 and 10. Only 3 and 8 satisfy both conditions.

Write and expand the factors.
x2 + 11x + 24 = (x + 3)(x + 8)

The middle products are 8x and 3x; they combine to 11x.

Make sign decisions before searching
Constant c	Middle coefficient b	Signs in the factors
Positive	Positive	Both positive
Positive	Negative	Both negative
Negative	Either	Opposite signs; the greater magnitude sets the sign of the sum.

For x² − 9x + 20, the product is positive and sum negative: use −4 and −5. For x² + x − 20, use 5 and −4. The same magnitudes can create different trinomials because the signs change the sum and product.

WORKED EXAMPLE

Factor a trinomial with opposite signs

Factor x² − 2x − 35.

Use opposite signs because the product is negative.
(−7)(5) = −35

The larger magnitude must be negative to produce a negative middle coefficient.

Check the signed sum.
−7 + 5 = −2

This matches the coefficient of x.

Write and verify the answer.
x2 − 2x − 35 = (x − 7)(x + 5)

Expanding gives x² + 5x − 7x − 35, which simplifies to the original.

Show why your factor pair works

One legitimate method is to split the middle term, group the terms, and remove the shared binomial. For x² + 7x + 12, enter the full intermediate expression—not just two numbers.

Build an intermediate step

Split the middle term into two terms that will allow grouping. Keep the complete expression.

Do not stop after taking out the GCF

Factor 3x² + 21x + 36 completely.

Remove the numerical GCF.
3x2 + 21x + 36 = 3(x2 + 7x + 12)

This is equivalent, but the trinomial inside can still be factored.

Factor the inside monic trinomial.
x2 + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4)

The pair multiplies to 12 and adds to 7.

Keep the outside factor.
3x2 + 21x + 36 = 3(x + 3)(x + 4)

Dropping the 3 would change every coefficient. Verify the entire product.

4.1 Roots, estimates and irrational numbers

Read root notation, locate non-perfect roots and compare real numbers in forms that do not look alike.

What the root symbol asks

In n√a, the index n asks which power must recover the radicand a. When no index is printed, the index is 2.

Radicand
The expression under the radical sign.
Index
The root being taken: square, cube, fourth, and so on.
Bracket before estimating

To locate √52, use neighbouring perfect squares.

7² = 49 < 52 < 64 = 8²

therefore 7 < √52 < 8

Since 52 is closer to 49 than to 64, an estimate a little above 7 is reasonable. A calculator can refine the decimal after the bracket is established.

Rational or irrational?

A rational number can be written as a fraction of integers with a nonzero denominator. Its decimal terminates or repeats. A non-perfect square root such as √52 is irrational; its decimal neither terminates nor repeats.

Try the reasoning before the decimal

Locate ∛90 without a calculator. Since 4³ = 64 and 5³ = 125, the value lies between 4 and 5. Now decide whether it is closer to 4 or 5 by comparing 90 with the two perfect cubes.

Check the reasoning
Order unlike-looking real numbers

Order 3.6, √13, 11/3. Use one comparable form without replacing exact values permanently.

Estimate only for comparison.

√13 ≈ 3.606 and 11/3 ≈ 3.667.

Write the order using the original forms.

3.6 < √13 < 11/3

Repair: roots are not division

The index in ∛64 does not mean 64 ÷ 3. It asks for the number whose third power is 64. Check a proposed root by raising it to the index.

u4-43.text:
4.3 Product, quotient and zero exponent laws

Use repeated multiplication to explain why exponents add, subtract or become zero.

Start from the same base
Situation	Law	Restriction
Multiply like bases	aman = am+n	Like base required
Divide like bases	am ÷ an = am−n	a ≠ 0
Zero exponent	a0 = 1	a ≠ 0
Separate coefficients from variable powers

(12x⁷y³) ÷ (3x²y³)

= 4x⁷⁻²y³⁻³

= 4x⁵

The coefficient division and each like-base exponent calculation are separate decisions. The original denominator also tells us x ≠ 0 and y ≠ 0.

A common error

Exponent laws describe multiplication and division. They do not allow x² + x³ to become x⁵.

Explain the laws with expanded factors

For b⁵ ÷ b², cancel two common factors from five:

(b·b·b·b·b)/(b·b) = b·b·b = b³, b ≠ 0

This explains subtraction of exponents and preserves the original denominator restriction.

Handle several bases independently

Simplify (18a⁷b⁴)/(6a²b⁶).

Divide coefficients.

18 ÷ 6 = 3.

Subtract exponents for each like base.

a⁷/a² = a⁵ and b⁴/b⁶ = b⁻².

Use positive exponents.

3a⁵/b², a ≠ 0, b ≠ 0

Repair: laws require multiplication or division

x² + x⁵ cannot be simplified because the variable parts are unlike terms. By contrast, x²·x⁵ = x⁷. Name the operation before choosing a law.

Use the exponent law lab to test the structure.

u4-45.text:
4.5 Negative exponents and reciprocals

Read a negative exponent as a reciprocal instruction, not as a negative value.

Why the reciprocal appears

The quotient law predicts a² ÷ a⁵ = a⁻³. Cancelling repeated factors gives 1/a³. Therefore:

a−n = 1/an, a ≠ 0

Rewrite using positive exponents

(3x⁻²)/(2y⁻³)

= (3y³)/(2x²)

The factors with negative exponents cross the fraction bar. The coefficient 3/2 does not invert because its exponent was not negative.

State restrictions from the original expression

When variables occur in denominators or carry negative exponents, zero is excluded. Keep restrictions from the original expression even if later simplification hides a denominator.

Move factors, not signs

Rewrite 5p⁻³/q⁻². The exponent signs tell where each powered factor belongs:

5p⁻³/q⁻² = 5q²/p³

The expression is not negative. Its value depends on p and q.

Evaluate a negative rational power

Evaluate (−2/3)⁻³.

Use the reciprocal.

(−3/2)³.

Apply the odd power.

−27/8

The negative sign remains because the exponent is odd.

Repair: preserve original restrictions

Even if x⁴/x⁴ simplifies to 1, the original quotient required x ≠ 0. Simplification cannot make a previously illegal value legal.

Review the reciprocal checklist before the mastery task.

u4-support-library.text:
Worked support library

Open only the lesson you need. Each guide names a decision, shows the mathematics and points back to a fresh task.

Support by lesson
4.1 · Bracket and classify a root

Find perfect powers immediately below and above the radicand. For √85, use 9²=81 and 10²=100, so 9<√85<10. Since 85 is not a perfect square, √85 is irrational.

Return to Lesson 4.1
4.2 · Simplify and convert radical forms
4.3 · Product, quotient and zero laws

Name the operation before changing exponents. Multiplication adds; division subtracts; a nonzero base divided by itself gives exponent zero and value 1. Treat each base independently and keep original denominator restrictions.

Return to Lesson 4.3
4.4 · Powers of grouped expressions
4.5 · Negative exponents

A negative exponent is a reciprocal instruction. Move only the powered factor across the fraction bar, then make its exponent positive. Read excluded values from the original expression before simplifying.

Return to Lesson 4.5
4.6 · Fractional exponents
4.7 · Multi-step exponent laws
4.8 · Choose a root in context
Return to a different fresh demonstration

Opening support helps learning and can reduce practice credit on the active lesson task. It never erases work or permanently lowers mastery. After repair, use the course’s next fresh task to show the skill independently.
